chapters.title: Chapter 1 - The Memorial
chapters.summary_simple: Chapter 1 begins at a memorial service in Liberia. Bendu Lewis remembers family, loss, and Granny May.
chapters.summary_detailed: Chapter 1 begins at a memorial service for Catherine Mae Tyler Lewis, also called Granny May. She died almost ten years ago during the Liberian civil war and her body was never found. Her family holds a service with an empty casket containing her portrait, her Bible, family pictures, a picture of her husband Samuel Lewis in a white rose, and the Liberian flag. The main character is Bendu Lewis, Granny May's granddaughter. Bendu is in deep pain because she was the last person to see her grandmother alive. She remembers how Granny May saved her. During the war Bendu was pushing her sick grandmother in a dirty, rusty wheelbarrow as they escaped from Charlie Town. Everyone was running for their lives. People shouted at Bendu to leave the old woman and save herself. Along the road, she saw abandoned babies crying, small children being trampled, and old and sick people left behind crying for help. Bendu said she would never leave her. Then Granny May died. An old man told Bendu, 'You did well to stay with your Ma. God bless you.' Immediately after, about thirty fighters appeared. They were not the official Liberian army. Their leaders were Commander Cobra and Samson. Bendu was tired of the war and wanted to die to join her late fiance Jonah. She was not afraid. The fighters mocked her and ordered her to follow them. When she refused, Samson hit her finger hard with his gun and broke it. The men dragged her away screaming. She fainted from pain, hunger and shock. When she woke up, it was dark and the fighters were setting up camp in the woods. Back at the memorial service, Bendu is surrounded by family and friends but she feels alone. She has a secret about one year with the fighters and fears her family will not forgive her if they know.
chapters.theme: War trauma, family love, loss, survival, forgiveness
chapters.setting: Liberia - Memorial service and Charlie Town escape during civil war

chapters.title: Chapter 2 - In The Cause of The People
chapters.summary_simple: Moses Varney arrives at the Temple of Justice in Monrovia for an important case. He meets his street boys Simeon and Alphonso.
chapters.summary_detailed: This chapter is about Moses Varney, a lawyer. It is 1986 in Monrovia. Varney is in a hurry. Lives are at stake and he must get to the Temple of Justice. He is in his old blue Pajero with his driver and bodyguard, Weah. On his dashboard is a bumper sticker from the 1980 coup that says IN THE CAUSE OF THE PEOPLE, THE STRUGGLE CONTINUES. Weah asks him, 'Barrister, are you sure you want to do this?' Varney checks the sticker and says yes. He parks at the Temple of Justice near Capitol Bypass. A group of teenage street boys are hanging around the parking lot. They see him and shout 'Brother V! Father! Brother V!' They are his boys. The leader is Simeon, and Alphonso is with him. Weah tries to chase them away, saying 'Get away from the car!' But Varney stops him and says 'Weah, these are my boys.' He is happy to see them. Simeon and Alphonso have grown. Varney looks at them and remembers his own childhood. At age 11, he lost both his parents in a terrible bus accident on the road from Sanniquellie to Monrovia. The bus was a small minibus but it was overloaded with many passengers, market produce, bags, chickens, a goat and even a pig. The driver was reckless. The bus fell into a ravine. Many people died, including his parents. About ten people died. After the accident, his two sisters were taken by relatives, and he was sent to his uncle in Monrovia. That experience changed his life forever. Now looking at Simeon, Alphonso and the other street boys who are young, jobless and hopeless, he feels their pain. He promises Simeon, 'I won't forget you.' He walks towards the Judiciary wing of the Temple of Justice. He is thinking about Liberia. He thinks that the country's leaders are often surprised by how bad the system is when they face it themselves. He believes there can be no peace without justice and equity for the masses. He believes the people must rise and liberate themselves. With new determination, he knocks on a large ornate door in the Judiciary wing.
chapters.theme: Justice, Youth Unemployment, Childhood Trauma, Social Equity, The Struggle Continues
chapters.setting: Temple of Justice, Capitol Bypass, Monrovia, Liberia, 1986
chapters.moral_lesson: True peace cannot exist without justice and equity. No justice, no peace.
